title: The Number of Good Subsets
statement:
A subset of the integer array `nums` is any choice of positions to keep (keeping all or none is allowed); two subsets count as different when they keep different sets of positions, even if the kept values are equal. A subset is **good** when the product of its kept values can be written as a product of one or more primes that are all different from each other. In other words, the product must be greater than `1` and no prime may divide it twice.

Return the number of good subsets of `nums`, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
notes:
## Intuition

Listing every subset is hopeless for 10^5 values, but the values only go up to 30. A good product never repeats a prime, so every value used must itself be **square-free** (4, 8, 9, 12, 16, 18, 20, 24, 25, 27 and 28 are useless) and the chosen values must have pairwise disjoint prime sets. Below 30 there are only ten primes, so a set of used primes fits in a 10-bit mask, and we can count subsets per mask, processing each distinct value once and weighting it by how many times it occurs. The value `1` adds no primes: each copy can be kept or not, doubling every count, but it cannot make a subset good on its own.

## Approach

1. Count occurrences of each value in `count`.
2. `dp[state]` = number of ways to pick values whose primes are exactly `state`. Start `dp[0]` at `2^count[1]` (any choice of the 1s).
3. For each value `x` from 2 to 30 that occurs, build its prime `mask` and skip it if it is not `squareFree`.
4. For every `state` containing `mask`, from high to low, add `dp[state ^ mask] * count[x]`: choose one of the `count[x]` copies on top of a selection using the other primes. Going downward means each value is used at most once.
5. Sum `dp[state]` over all non-empty `state` into `total`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]`. One `1` gives `dp[0] = 2`. Value 2 has mask `0b01` and sets `dp[0b01] = dp[0] * 1 = 2`. Value 3 has mask `0b10` and sets `dp[0b11] = dp[0b01] * 1 = 2` and `dp[0b10] = dp[0] * 1 = 2`. Value 4 is divisible by `2 * 2` and is skipped. `total = 2 + 2 + 2 = 6`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + 30 · 2^10): counting, then a fixed amount of work per distinct value.
- Space: O(2^10) for `dp`.

## Pitfalls

- Do not count the 1s as a good subset: only non-empty prime sets are summed.
- Copies of the same value cannot both be chosen (they share primes), so multiply by `count[x]` instead of looping over copies.
- Iterate `state` downward so a value is not reused within its own update, and reduce modulo `10^9 + 7` after every product (in Java and C use a 64-bit type for `dp[...] * count[x]`).

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD` | the modulus `10^9 + 7` |
| `PRIMES` | the ten primes up to 29; bit `p` stands for `PRIMES[p]` |
| `count` | how many times each value 1..30 occurs |
| `dp` | ways to reach each set of used primes |
| `x`, `mask`, `squareFree` | current value, its prime bits, and whether it repeats a prime |
| `state`, `total` | a prime set being updated, and the final sum |

narration.4: Only values 1..30 occur, so count how often each one appears.
narration.9: One dp entry per set of the ten primes, encoded as a 10-bit mask.
narration.10: Before any value is chosen, the only reachable prime set is the empty one.
narration.11: Each 1 can be kept or dropped without adding primes...
narration.12: ...so every copy doubles the number of ways to reach the empty set.
narration.15: Consider each other value once, together with all of its copies.
narration.21: Check every prime below 30 against x.
narration.22: If p squared divides x, any product containing x repeats p.
narration.26: Record that p divides x in its prime mask.
narration.29: A value with a repeated prime can never be part of a good subset.
narration.32: Walk prime sets from high to low so x is added at most once per selection.
narration.33: Only sets that contain all of x's primes can end with x.
narration.34: Add the ways to pick the remaining primes, times the copies of x to choose from.
narration.40: Every non-empty prime set is a good product.
narration.43: Return the total number of good subsets modulo 10^9 + 7.
